reviews.review:
This is probably going to be a bit of a surprise, coming from me. For context: Double Spoiler is one of my favorite Touhou games, and Impossible Spellcard is my favorite. So why did a fangame photogame with the ability to take a helpful item into any scene leave me negative?

It mostly comes down to this being a photogame that seemed afraid of being a photogame and wanted to be more of an ISC. A fundamental mechanic of the camera is that it deletes bullets in the frame, almost without exception. Flickerframe Shutter Festival has so many instances of bullets that don't that I lost count of how many times it happened, and lasers are never canceled. One particularly egregious scene is 10 photos on unique patterns, where the bullets are all uncancellable, and there's no spawn protection so the next wave can and will spawn directly on top of you if you're where it will spawn. There were a couple instances of what are effectively "survival cards" where you just need one photo, but need to survive a long time to get there. This is a fine idea in concept, but in practice these are memorize or die traps where you have to push a couple seconds later to see what happens next to be able to already be responding to it.

Many scenes are very gimmicky, and at least for me most of these didn't land. I did like the one where your photos get deleted though! The one that stands out the most - in a bad way - I had to ask a friend how it actually worked, because it requires pressing X (to change orientation) to change the currently active laser to match the one that starts reversing, or else you can't take a picture of the boss. Every time you die, a partner character says one of a few canned lines, and some of these are hints (or directly telling you what to do) for the current scene. On this scene? All you get is "this will be a true test of concentration!" which isn't helpful! The worst of these to me was a lategame scene where the comment was "pay attention to the order and this will be easy" or something like that, but the actual dodging and moving from point to point was very difficult.

Did I say very difficult? I meant that it was difficult, and sometimes you randomly just get walled or trapped. This happens quite frequently, including on the scene that took me the most attempts in the entire game: 13-10. The first phase is ridiculous unless you find a safespot that only sometimes works, the second phase will wall you frequently (and expects you to know exactly what to do the moment it starts), the third phase is unfair with the speed of some random bullets (and a tracking laser that will instantly reverse direction and aim at you if you get too far ahead), and the final phase is immune to photos for like 10 seconds and again, if you don't know what to do in advance you will die and it will take 30 minutes or more to get back there. Really unfair pattern with no redeeming qualities. It really seems like this is a game that wasn't made by or tested by players who were at the level of difficulty they were trying to make.

Control-wise I kept not getting photos when trying to take them, in a way that doesn't happen in StB or DS, though I couldn't tell you why. Maybe it had to do with the constant framedrops I was getting, because on top of all of those other design issues, Flickerframe Shutter Festival is extremely badly optimized.

That's not to say this is all bad, though. There are A LOT of characters here, a lot of novel ideas, the helpful item mechanic is a nice addition (though one is clearly best), and if you really really want another photogame, and have played the rest (including Tri-Focuser, another fangame), then you can't do better than Flickerframe Shutter Festival. An amazing concept, executed poorly.
